title: LLM-Powered Interactive Graph Search: A Scalable and Practical Approach

statements.text: (Interactive Graph Search [7, 45]) Given a classification hierarchy 𝐻 , an oracle, and a query entity 𝜑, the goal of Interactive Graph Search is to identify the target concept 𝑡𝜑 with the maximum accuracy and the minimum interaction cost. The cost of the IGS algorithm is conventionally measured by the total number of questions asked (i.e., number of interactions with the oracle). In previous settings, the effectiveness of algorithms is rarely considered, as the oracle is assumed to be perfect, meaning it can always answer any query correctly. (Limitations of Existing IGS Framework) The presence of both ambiguous nodes and overlapping nodes poses significant effectiveness challenges for existing binary-search-based and greedy-based IGS algorithms in real-world settings. Specifically, reachability queries on ambiguous nodes often result in incorrect answers from the oracle, misleading subsequent searches toward incorrect subgraphs that exclude the target node. For overlapping nodes, even correct query answers from the oracle may still direct searches into subgraphs that deviate from the target node. It is important to note that ambiguous nodes and overlapping nodes are independent characteristics, and a single node can possess both simultaneously. 3.2 Large-Language-Model-Based Oracles Reflecting on the role of oracles, they should serve as an independent external resource capable of comprehending the relationship between an entity and the queried concept. Although crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk1 present a viable option, the time and effort required to interact with crowdworkers are often impractical. This is an important reason why the perfect oracle which always provides correct answers is extensively used to simplify the design of previous oracles [8, 45, 57, 63, 65]. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has provided new opportunities for addressing the IGS problem in practical settings. proofs.text: Assume 𝑄𝑟 (𝑞) = 𝑌𝑒𝑠, which implies that node 𝑞 can reach the target node 𝑡𝜑 . For any 𝑤 ∈ 𝑎𝑛𝑐 (𝑞), there exists a path from 𝑤 to 𝑞. Consequently, a path from 𝑤 to 𝑡𝜑 passing through 𝑞 exists, thus 𝑄𝑟 (𝑤) = 𝑌𝑒𝑠 holds. For the second part, assume 𝑄𝑟 (𝑞) = 𝑁𝑜. If there exists a node 𝑤 ∈ 𝑑𝑒𝑠 (𝑞) such that 𝑄𝑟 (𝑤) = 𝑌𝑒𝑠, then 𝑞 must also be able to reach 𝑡𝜑 , implying 𝑄𝑟 (𝑞) = 𝑌𝑒𝑠, which is a contradiction. Therefore, 𝑄𝑟 (𝑤) = 𝑁𝑜 holds. □
